0: Bad form is easy to fall into when exercising, and without a coach to guide you, can AI take the coach's place?
1: If the follow-along session is recorded, can AI first help us spot the obvious differences? This chapter follows that idea to build an AI fitness-coach example.
2: First find the body keypoints — shoulders, elbows, hips, knees — in the video, turning the movement into comparable data; then combine joint angles with when each movement happens to find the differences between the student and the coach's demonstration. Finally, hand those results to a multimodal model together with the corresponding frames to try to generate feedback that is easier to understand.
4: The first step in analysing a fitness movement is to let the computer recognise the body's pose in the video. A video is essentially a series of images. To a computer the raw image is just pixels: it does not know where the shoulders, knees or ankles are, so we first use human pose estimation to identify the main body positions in each frame.
5: This section uses MediaPipe Pose for body pose recognition. MediaPipe Pose can detect 33 body keypoints, including the shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles.

24: Besides the difference in body size, the coach and the student usually do not move at exactly the same speed. For example, when the coach has already reached the bottom of a squat, the student may still be on the way down. Comparing the same timestamps in two videos naively can mistake a difference in rhythm for a difference in pose. For videos recorded in sync you can compare directly by frame. If the coach and student come from two separate videos, you can use Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align them in time. The basic idea of DTW is to find a more reasonable correspondence from how the two movement sequences change. 29: DTW then finds, from these distances, an alignment path with a smaller cumulative cost, so that two videos with different rhythm can be compared correspondingly. In this section's experiment the coach's and student's videos were recorded in sync, so they can be compared frame by frame without extra DTW.

48: The pose-estimation analysis above already gives the concrete differences between the student's movement and the coach's demonstration at the level of keypoints and joint angles. These differences are numeric: precise but lacking semantic understanding, and hard to turn directly into feedback a trainee can understand and act on. This section shows how, on top of those quantitative results, to bring in a multimodal large model to understand the movement and generate natural-language feedback. The video information is as follows:
51: Real follow-along fitness videos are usually not one movement repeated but several different movements one after another, possibly with preparation, rest and transition segments in between. If you ignore that and hand the whole video's keypoint data and deviation results to a large model at once, two problems arise. First, different movements care about different joints and criteria (a squat focuses on knee and hip angles, a curl on the elbow angle), so mixing them lets the criteria interfere. Second, asking the model to both identify the current movement and evaluate its quality in one inference greatly increases prompt complexity and the model's cognitive load, especially for smaller models, and easily lowers output quality. So before evaluating, this experiment first recognises and segments the movement, dividing the video into several relatively independent segments of a single movement type, then analyses each segment separately.
52: This experiment samples frames from the video at a fixed interval (say every 2 seconds) and feeds only the coach's side into the multimodal large model to judge which movement the frame belongs to (such as “dumbbell squat”, “dumbbell curl”, “lateral raise” or “bent-over row”). Because visual classification has some error rate, using frame-by-frame results directly easily produces scattered fragments (for example, one frame in a continuous movement being misjudged as another class). So after obtaining the sequence of classification labels for consecutive frames, a sliding-window majority vote is first applied to remove isolated misjudged frames; consecutive frames with the same label are then merged into one movement segment; finally segments that are too short are merged into a neighbour, giving the final segmentation. 56: After movement recognition and segmentation, the system knows which movements the video contains and the time range of each. Next, the joint-angle deviations from the pose analysis must be matched to those segments and turned into movement evaluations and improvement suggestions the trainee can understand.
57: The pose analysis mainly produces quantitative information: joint angles, deviation sizes and when the deviations occur. That data shows “how much” the student differs from the coach, but it is not intuitive for an ordinary user. This stage reorganises the deviation data by movement segment, grouping the pose deviations and keyframes belonging to the same movement, and hands them to the multimodal large model separately. Here the multimodal model does not re-judge from the video whether a movement is standard; it takes the quantitative pose-estimation results as the main basis and, with the keyframes, observes movement range, body posture and stability. For example, when the system has already detected a clear difference in elbow angle between student and coach, the large model can use the corresponding frames to explain how that difference shows up in the actual movement and turn the angle data into more intuitive training advice. The evaluation also proceeds segment by segment: for different movements such as the dumbbell curl or the lateral raise, the corresponding deviation data and keyframes are supplied, so the model analyses one clear movement at a time. Compared with giving the model several movements from the whole video at once, this reduces interference between movements and makes the evaluation more focused. The core logic is implemented below:

61: The movement recognition, pose analysis and multimodal evaluation above mainly answer how well the movements were performed in one session. For an AI fitness coach, combining the training process and historical data can extend single-movement correction into more continuous training analysis and personalised guidance. Data from different sessions can be saved and linked into a long-term training record. For example, continuously recording the joint-angle deviations, movement stability and completion of the same movement lets you compare how a student changes after many sessions. If a deviation gradually shrinks, the movement is being mastered better; if a problem persists, later sessions can keep reminding and focusing on it. That extends the AI fitness coach's subject from one session to a continuous training process. On that basis you can also bring in the user's training goals and personal information. For example, combining goals such as muscle gain, fat loss or posture improvement, plus training frequency, duration and history, with the movement analysis lets the large model generate advice that fits the individual better. The AI fitness coach then does not just correct a single movement on the spot but can gradually form a complete flow from movement recognition and pose quantification to movement evaluation, training records and personalised guidance.
